title: Buying the Training Data Instead of Taking It
hook: Google is reportedly offering Hollywood studios big money to train on their films. That's an admission about how the last decade of scraping worked.
key_points: Google has reportedly approached major Hollywood studios about licensing copyrighted material for AI training, per The Verge.
The offer is cash for training rights — the alternative path to scraping-then-litigating.
Licensing favors whoever can pay, entrenching the largest labs against smaller and open-source ones.
The Verge's argument: Google needs the studios' catalog more than the studios need Google's AI.
Studios weigh short-term payment against training a system that could compete with them.
content_html: Google has reportedly been approaching Hollywood's biggest studios about licensing deals — permission to train its AI models on copyrighted films and shows, in exchange for what The Verge describes as massive piles of cash. On paper it's a win for everyone: studios get paid for archives that were previously being used without consent, and Google gets legally clean data.
extra_html:
That framing skips the interesting part, which is what the offer concedes. For a decade the working assumption at most labs was that publicly reachable material was fair game and the lawsuits could be dealt with later. Paying up front is a different bet — that the scraping path is getting too expensive, legally and reputationally, to keep running.

It also quietly reshapes competition. Licensed data is data you can afford, and the labs that can write nine-figure checks for a studio catalog are a very short list. A world where good training data must be bought is a world where the incumbents stay incumbents, and open-source and academic projects fall further behind.

The studios' own calculation, as The Verge frames it, is that they hold the stronger hand — Google needs their catalog more than they need Google's AI. A licensing fee arrives once; the model it helps train doesn't expire.

related.title: The US Government Filed on the AI Company's Side
related.hook: The Trump administration intervened in the New York Times' copyright case against OpenAI — arguing for the lab. That's a new kind of pressure on the courts.

related.title: Two Music Giants Sue an AI Lab Over Tens of Thousands of Songs
related.hook: Sony Music and Warner Chappell are suing Anthropic over copyrighted works — and the damages math shows why these training-data cases are existential, not incidental.

related.title: Who Owns AI's Output?
related.hook: You typed the prompt, the AI made the image — so who owns it? The law is genuinely unsettled, and the answer depends on where you are and how much was really you.

flashcards.prompt: What are the two routes AI labs take to copyrighted training data?
flashcards.back_html: Scrape it and defend the lawsuits, or pay to license it up front. Google's reported approach to the studios is the second route.

flashcards.prompt: Who is disadvantaged if licensing becomes the industry norm?

choices.text: Smaller labs and open-source projects that can't afford to pay for catalogs
The largest AI companies, who lose access to free data
Rights holders, who lose control of their work

flashcards.explanation_html: Paying for data is a cost the biggest labs can absorb and smaller competitors cannot — so licensing raises the barrier to entry.

flashcards.prompt: Why might a studio hesitate even at a large licensing fee?
flashcards.back_html: The payment is one-time; the model it trains is permanent. They'd be funding a tool that could eventually generate the kind of content they sell.
